Drums: the Groove MIDI Dataset's counts (Google LLC, CC BY 4.0), maestro/data/grooves.json (task 3.3)
Harmony: our counts from the Rock Corpus (de Clercq and Temperley, CC BY 4.0), maestro/data/rock.json (task 3.4d)

The guitar, the lead and the parts: Wikipedia's "Power chord", "Palm mute", "Pentatonic scale", "String bending", "Verse-chorus form" and "Arena rock" (CC BY-SA 4.0), the ideas in our own words (task 3.4d)
80s arena rock, the tempo kept at 130: DadCraft, Oct 26

The second round (DadCraft, Oct 26): "double bass pedals and dueling guitars, akin to Bill and Ted": 80s hair metal and shred, the tempo 150; Wikipedia's "Double bass drum", "Twin lead guitar", "Shred guitar" and "Guitar solo" (CC BY-SA 4.0), the ideas in our own words

feel.why: Straight, driving: big accents on the beat.

leading.why: Power chords slide as one shape.

progressions.why: 80s arena rock (DadCraft, Oct 26), from our Rock Corpus counts (maestro/data/rock.json): I, IV and V carry most of the time; around the era (1975-1991) half the songs reach for bVII, a third for bVI. Four-bar loops a chord a bar: the anthem's I-V-vi-IV, the double plagal (bVII to IV to I), the I-IV vamp turned home by V, the fifties loop; in a minor key the climb home through bVI and bVII. Loops mostly come round as written; every phrase lands home, so the lead's last note sits on its own chord.

anthem.why: the big major loop: home, the fifth, the relative minor, the fourth

double plagal.why: the flat seventh to the fourth to home: rock's own way round, the era's most borrowed chord

rock vamp.chords: I IV | I IV | I IV | I V
rock vamp.why: the commonest vamp in the counts, home and the fourth, turned by the fifth

fifties.why: the old loop the ballads keep

climb home.why: the arena lift: the flat sixth and seventh climbing back to home

aeolian climb.why: for a minor key: home, then the two chords that climb back to it

minor rock.why: for a minor key: rocking down the steps under home and back

dark vamp.why: for a minor key: home held, then the climb

members.why: 80s hair metal and shred (DadCraft, Oct 26): two distortion guitars on power chords, left and right (the pad sits out), a picked bass, two overdriven leads, one each side, singing alone in a verse, in twin harmony in a chorus, trading licks in a duel; double bass drums in the loud parts.

guitar.why: Power chords doubled left and right, each in its own octave: palm-muted chugs in a verse, open 8ths to build, big ringing chords and the dotted push in a chorus.

patterns.why: Each hit [16th, 16ths or null (rings to the next), shape, now or ahead]; a group a part (arrange).

chugs.why: palm-muted 8ths on the root and fifth

chug and push.why: muted 8ths, the and of 4 pushing the next chord in

gallop.why: an 8th and two 16ths a beat, the bass locked to it

push 8ths.why: open 8ths, the and of 4 pushing in, the bass locked to it

drive gallop.why: the gallop opened up, an 8th and two 16ths a beat over the double bass, the bass locked to it

anthem.why: the dotted push, three-three-two, the and of 4 into the next chord

ringing.why: big chords left to ring, struck each half bar

bass.why: A picked bass driving 8ths on the root, locked to the kick; the octave pumping when loud, the push on the and of 4; sparser in a quiet verse.

octave pump.why: the root and its octave in 8ths

eighths and push.why: 8ths, the and of 4 pushing the next chord in

verse roots.why: the root on 1 and 3 with pickups

held roots.why: the root held each half bar under a quiet verse

melody.why: Two overdriven leads, one each side, on the pentatonic: the first sings a verse alone; in a chorus the second joins a third under it (twin harmony); in a duel they trade shred licks (runs, pedal licks, sweeps), the turns getting shorter, and land home together. Held notes bend up into place, long ones shake.

drums.why: GMD's rock drummers with double bass (written from theory: GMD has none): the hat in a verse, the ride or the crash in a chorus; in the loud parts both feet run 16ths or the gallop, and a burst of 16ths drives into some phrases; a snare build at a pre-chorus's end.

double.why: Both feet: kicks as a bar's 16ths, the loud parts that play them, bursts (% of the other phrases' last beats). Every run's kick at velocity 120, both feet even, on GM's Power kit (sound 16, a punchier kick), the bass an octave up out of their way (DadCraft, Oct 26: "i almost didn't hear the double bass pedal kicks").

gallop.why: an 8th and two 16ths a beat, with the guitars' gallop

arrange.why: Verse to chorus to the duel (Wikipedia's "Verse-chorus form", "Arena rock" and "Guitar solo", in our own words): the play opens on a verse, palm-muted, one lead singing; loud phrases are the chorus (big open chords, the two leads in twin harmony), driven in 8ths, or after a chorus the duel (the solo pulled forward from task 3.6: the two leads trading licks); a quiet section leading into a loud one most often builds through a pre-chorus; some section ends stop.

verse.why: the lead sings over palm-muted chugs

chorus.why: big open chords, the two leads in twin harmony on the hook

drive.why: a loud phrase driven in open 8ths

pre-chorus.why: open 8ths building, the snare doubling up into the chorus

duel.why: the two leads trading licks over the gallop and the double bass

judge.why: Written from GMD's rock drummers (maestro/data/grooves.json, CC BY 4.0) and Wikipedia's "Power chord", "Palm mute", "String bending", "Double bass drum" and "Twin lead guitar", not from the entry's patterns.

steps: GMD rock: every common groove's snare on 2 and 4

notes: GMD rock: 2-4 a bar; Wikipedia, "Double bass drum": 16th runs in the loud parts
steps: GMD rock: every common groove's kick on the one

velocity: GMD rock: hats near 95 on the beat, 70-80 on the and, near 50 on the 16ths
triplets: GMD rock: straight takes, the odd triplet fill

voices: Wikipedia, "Power chord": the root and fifth, no third
chord tones: Wikipedia, "Power chord": the chord's root and fifth
syncopation: Wikipedia, "Palm mute": driving 8ths on the beat; the odd push
register: Wikipedia, "Power chord": low on the guitar's bottom strings, from E2

notes: GMD rock and Wikipedia, "Arena rock": a bass in 8ths locked to the kick
chord tones: the bass on the root under power chords
register: Wikipedia, "Bass guitar": its lowest string E1

slides: Wikipedia, "String bending": held notes bent up into place
chord tones: Open Music Theory, "Embellishing tones" (CC BY-SA 4.0): the strong beats take the chord's tones; the pentatonic's passing notes
top: docs/taste.md, "Failures to check for": the melody must stay on top; the twin lead a third under it (Wikipedia, "Twin lead guitar")
